summary: Specifies EAP-PSK, an experimental Extensible Authentication Protocol method for mutual authentication and session key derivation from a pre-shared key. Once both sides authenticate, it provides a protected channel.

plainLanguage.summary: Two devices already share a secret password. EAP-PSK lets each prove to the other it knows it, then makes a private code for chatting. It is an experiment, not a standard.

subtitle: Lightweight authentication for wireless networks using only a shared secret.

tldr.problem: Wireless networks need a way for two parties who already share a secret to prove they know it and establish a protected channel, without complex infrastructure or expensive cryptography.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-PSK uses AES-128 and a fixed message pattern to derive two authentication keys from the pre-shared key, then runs an authenticated key exchange to prove knowledge and create session keys.
tldr.outcome: Two parties mutually authenticate and can exchange result confirmations over a protected channel, though the protocol does not offer perfect forward secrecy or identity protection.

today: RFC 4764 is Experimental and remains unpromoted. EAP-PSK is not widely deployed but has been studied for wireless LANs and VPN environments. The design principles have influenced later work, though other EAP methods (such as EAP-TLS) remain more commonly deployed.

sections.title: Design Goals and Context
sections.content:
EAP-PSK is an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method designed for networks where two parties share a pre-shared key (PSK). EAP is a framework for carrying authentication data over networks like 802.11 wireless LANs. Most existing EAP methods in the standards track (MD5-Challenge, OTP, GTC) are deprecated for security reasons, and methods requiring infrastructure (like EAP-SIM) or IPR-encumbered algorithms are not suitable for all deployments.

EAP-PSK prioritizes simplicity, choosing a single cryptographic primitive (AES-128) to avoid complex negotiations and make it suitable for low-power devices. It is designed for use over insecure networks where an attacker controls the communication channel. The protocol deliberately trades advanced features like identity protection and perfect forward secrecy for ease of implementation and deployment. It was developed at France Telecom R&D in 2003–2004 and is published as Experimental.
sections.plainLanguage: When both sides already know a secret, EAP-PSK proves you both really know it without needing a fancy server, and then creates a secret code just for this conversation.

sections.title: Key Hierarchy and Cryptographic Design
sections.content:
EAP-PSK is built on a key hierarchy. The Pre-Shared Key (PSK) is a 16-byte credential shared in advance. Rather than use the PSK directly, it is used once to derive two long-lived static keys: the Authentication Key (AK), used to prove both sides know the PSK, and the Key-Derivation Key (KDK), used to generate session keys. This separation protects the PSK from exposure and strengthens the protocol's design.

From KDK, three types of keying material are derived: the Transient EAP Key (TEK), a 16-byte session key protecting the EAP conversation itself using AES-128 in EAX mode (an authenticated-encryption mode); the Master Session Key (MSK), a 64-byte key exported from the method and typically used to derive further keys for data protection; and the Extended Master Session Key (EMSK), another 64-byte key reserved for future uses and not given to third parties.

The key setup and authenticated key exchange are based on AKEP2, an established protocol. Cryptographic operations use AES-128 in modified counter mode for key derivation and EAX mode for the protected channel, avoiding invention of new primitives. This conservative approach uses algorithms that have been reviewed by the cryptographic community.
sections.plainLanguage: One secret password becomes multiple secret codes: one to prove you both know the original password, another to create the protected channel, and more for whatever comes next. All made from AES, which is well-trusted.

sections.title: Message Flow and Protected Channel
sections.content:
EAP-PSK exchanges four messages to authenticate and establish the protected channel. The first message is sent by the server (the authenticator or the backend server), containing a nonce and the server's NAI (Network Access Identifier). The second message, from the peer, echoes part of the first and includes a peer nonce. The third message contains an authentication tag proving the peer knows the PSK and carries encrypted key material. The fourth message confirms success or reports failure.

The fixed message format avoids Type-Length-Value (TLV) complexity and reduces implementation burden. After mutual authentication succeeds, the TEK establishes a Protected Channel using AES-128-EAX mode. This channel is used to exchange protected result indications (DONE_SUCCESS, DONE_FAILURE) rather than relying on unprotected EAP-Success and EAP-Failure packets, which can be spoofed. The channel also supports an optional extended authentication mechanism for future extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides send four messages: the server starts with a challenge, the peer responds, they both prove they know the secret, and the last message locks everything in place. Then they can chat inside a locked box.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limitations
sections.content:
EAP-PSK provides mutual authentication: both the peer and server prove to each other they know the PSK. It is resistant to dictionary attacks because the protocol operates on keys derived from a high-entropy PSK, not passwords. Integrity protection comes from message authentication codes (CMAC with AES-128). Replay protection is provided by nonces and sequence numbers. The protocol resists reflection attacks (where an attacker replays a message back to the sender) through its authenticated key exchange design. Confidentiality in the protected channel is offered by AES-128-EAX.

However, the protocol has intentional limitations. It does not offer Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS): if someone later learns the PSK, they can decrypt recorded sessions. It provides no Identity Protection; the peer's NAI is transmitted in the clear. It is not designed for password-based authentication; it requires a high-entropy pre-shared key. Denial-of-service resistance is limited: an attacker can consume resources by initiating many authentications. The protocol assumes a trusted channel for PSK establishment and does not protect key distribution.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP-PSK proves both sides are real and talks only in code, but if someone steals the password later, they can read old messages. It also does not hide who is talking, just that it is really them.

sections.title: Applicability and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
EAP-PSK is designed for environments where a pre-shared key has been distributed in advance, such as corporate VPNs or small office networks. It is particularly suitable for wireless LANs (802.11) because it is lightweight, requires no public-key infrastructure, and operates over any transport. The protocol is suitable for devices with limited processing power and memory.

The RFC cautions that derivation of a PSK from a human-chosen password is discouraged (see Appendix A), as this negates the high-entropy assumption and exposes the protocol to dictionary attacks. PSKs should be generated by random number generators. The protocol requires careful implementation to avoid side-channel attacks and must be used with an underlying BEEP or transport-layer security profile to protect the EAP conversation. For use in 802.11, underlying security profiles like TLS should be negotiated to provide the full security posture.

The IESG notes that this RFC is not a candidate for Internet Standard and is published for general information. Readers should exercise caution in evaluating the suitability of EAP-PSK for their specific applications.
sections.plainLanguage: EAP-PSK works best when both sides get the secret ahead of time through a safe channel. It is good for corporate networks and small setups where you can hand out passwords securely before anyone connects.

items.title: Mutual Authentication
items.text: Peer and server prove they know the PSK.

items.title: Protected Channel
items.text: Uses AES-128 in EAX mode for confidentiality and integrity.

items.title: No Perfect Forward Secrecy
items.text: Compromise of PSK reveals all session keys.

items.title: Simplicity
items.text: Single cryptographic primitive, fixed message format.
